item.title: Smartphone-Based Simulated Photometer for Teaching Spectrophotometry Using AI-Assisted Tools
item.description:
Abstract This study proposes an approach that uses generative artificial intelligence (AI) to develop a web application capable of interfacing with a smartphone camera and performing quantitative RGB-based chemical measurements. Using this method, students can readily convert their own smartphones into simple photometers for immediate use in the classroom. With teacher guidance, students employ AI agents to create HTML files that activate the smartphone camera and extract RGB values from captured images, converting light intensity measurements into absorbance data. Unlike conventional commercial software, which is generally immutable and operates as a closed system, this approach enables students to develop customized simulated photometers based on their unique design concepts by manipulating AI prompt inputs. By employing this approach, students are able to rapidly configure a simulated spectrophotometer utilizing solely their smartphones within the classroom environment, without the need for any additional external equipment, thereby enabling them to perform a range of simulated spectrophotometric experiments. By actively participating in the design of a simulated photometer and directly observing its operational process during hands-on manipulation, students can achieve a deeper understanding of the fundamental mechanisms and essential principles underlying spectrophotometry. item.title: Mathematics Preparation, Intrinsic Motivation, Self-Efficacy, and Achievement in General Chemistry II: A Structural Equation Modeling Study
item.description:
Abstract Introductory chemistry often functions as a gateway course for students pursuing STEM majors and science-related careers. Although mathematics preparation and self-efficacy are well-established predictors of general chemistry achievement, less is known about how these factors operate together with intrinsic motivation and about which types of intrinsic motivation are most closely linked to students’ self-efficacy. Guided by social cognitive theory and self-determination theory, this study used latent-variable structural equation modeling to examine how mathematics preparation, intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy explained the lecture grades of 299 students in a General Chemistry II course. The full model fit the data well and fit better than a restricted model that removed the path from intrinsic motivation to self-efficacy. Self-efficacy and mathematics preparation directly predicted lecture grades, and the model explained 22% of their variance, whereas intrinsic motivation was associated with achievement only indirectly, through its strong association with self-efficacy. Among the three types of intrinsic motivation, intrinsic motivation to accomplish was most strongly correlated with self-efficacy. item.title: Teaching the Periodic Table to Ninth-Grade Students through Game-Based Learning and a Contextualized Science–Technology–Society–Environment Approach
item.description:
Abstract Chemistry is often perceived as a challenging subject due to its abstract nature, particularly in topics such as the Periodic Table, where students frequently struggle with chemical symbolism and conceptual understanding. This study examined how a structured instructional approach combining teacher-led instruction, a contextualized Science–Technology–Society–Environment (STSE) perspective, and game-based activities supported ninth-grade students’ learning of the Periodic Table, motivation, and perceived skill development. The intervention included a contextualized text (“Chemical Elements and the Brain”), digital quizzes using Kahoot, and a teacher-designed board game (Tab2Elementar). The study involved 20 students and adopted a single-group exploratory mixed-methods design without a control group, combining quantitative data from pre- and post-tests with qualitative data from interviews, students’ written reflections, and classroom observations. Results indicate an overall improvement in students’ performance, with most students achieving medium normalized gains and showing progress in key curriculum-related learning outcomes concerning the Periodic Table, including the identification of groups 1, 2, 17, and 18, the distinction between metals and nonmetals, and the role of chemical elements in the human body. item.title: A Practical Guide to RNA NMR Spectral Analysis for Undergraduate Students
item.description:
Abstract Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a powerful analytical tool that can be used to determine the structures of both small organic molecules and large biomacromolecules. Many undergraduate students are exposed to NMR spectral analysis during organic chemistry courses, but few students have the opportunity to learn about biomacromolecular NMR spectral analysis. Here, we present a three-part practicum aimed at providing resources for faculty to introduce RNA structure and NMR analysis into existing upper-level courses. Students will begin by predicting an RNA secondary structure using a Web server that uses nearest neighbor parameters to estimate the folding stability. Then, students can verify the secondary structure using 1D NMR data. Students can then learn the iterative process of chemical shift assignments through the concurrent analysis of multiple 2D NMR spectra. Students will also be able to visualize the RNA tertiary structure, allowing them to connect the somewhat abstract NMR spectra with measurable interproton distances. Collectively, these activities are designed to develop representational competence and visual literacy by requiring students to translate between RNA sequence, secondary structure, tertiary structure, and experimental NMR data.

item.title: Divergent Pathways in Transacetalization Reactions of meso -Hydrobenzoin with Formaldehyde Diethyl Acetal, Acetaldehyde Diethyl Acetal, and Acetone Dimethyl Acetal: A Comparative Study Using NMR Spectroscopy
item.description:
Abstract The separate acid-catalyzed reactions of meso-hydrobenzoin at room temperature with molar excesses of three analogous acetals─formaldehyde diethyl acetal, acetaldehyde diethyl acetal, and acetone dimethyl acetal─were performed by three groups of students, with each group employing a different acetal. Students discovered that NMR spectral analysis of products from the reactions of meso-hydrobenzoin with the acetals of acetaldehyde and acetone indicated formation of the expected corresponding cyclic acetals (1,3-dioxolanes) via transacetalization; however, they found that reaction of meso-hydrobenzoin with the acetal of formaldehyde yielded the corresponding acyclic bis(ethoxymethyl) ether derivative. Students were asked to rationalize these divergent outcomes based on the relative stabilities of the resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion intermediates involved in the mechanisms of these reactions.

item.title: Hands-On Biosensor Construction with Polyphenol Oxidase: A Gateway to Interdisciplinary STEM Learning
item.description:
Abstract Biosensor development stands among the most dynamic and promising areas of contemporary scientific research, driven by its ability to deliver rapid, specific, and highly sensitive responses in analytically demanding contexts. For engineering undergraduates, exploring biochemical applications fosters the integration of knowledge across disciplines, enhancing their capacity to address complex real-world challenges. Such experiences are instrumental in shaping scientific, technical, and problem-solving skills essential to their future professional practice. This progress exerts a significant impact on critical domains such as healthcare, food safety, protection, pharmacology, biotechnology, and biosafety, among others. This laboratory activity focuses on the development of a biosensor for detecting phenolic compounds, employing tyrosinase as a bioreceptor through the catalytic oxidation of the target substrate. The enzymatic reaction is monitored in real-time using a light-dependent resistor (LDR) integrated with an Arduino Uno board. Once programmed, the system identifies the presence of phenolic compounds by measuring variations in light intensity generated by the redox reaction catalyzed by purified and immobilized tyrosinase. This activity highlights the advantages of using a purified enzyme immobilized in a biopolymer matrix to develop a biosensor for detecting and quantifying phenolic compounds. item.title: A Comprehensive Training Course from the Production of Membrane Bound Proteins to Single Particle Cryo-Electron Microscopy 3D Reconstruction
item.description:
Abstract Single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) has been firmly cemented as a routine technique in structural biology. CryoEM is especially prominent in the 3-dimensional structural study of membrane proteins. As cryoEM has seen high levels of adoption over the last 15 years, there is a great need to provide comprehensive training and a theoretical framework in this technique coupled with the biochemical tools required to purify proteins suitable for cryo-EM experiments. This manuscript details the graduate student rotation program developed for the Australian Research Council (ARC) Industrial Transformation and Training Centre, the Centre for Cryo-electron Microscopy of Membrane Proteins (CCeMMP), to train students in the essential skills required for determination of cryo-EM structures of membrane proteins.

item.title: Three Self-Fabricated Energy Conversion Demonstrators Based on Thermoelectric Generators, Hydrogen–Oxygen Fuel Cells, and Voice Recognition Control
item.description:
Abstract Chemical reactions and energy conversion are core concepts in secondary school chemistry. Chemical reactions are often accompanied by variations in energy. While energy is omnipresent in daily life, its transmission and conversion processes are intangible, which results in the lack of intuitive experiences of students with these concepts. In this paper, we have designed three chemical energy conversion demonstrators that illustrate the conversion of chemical energy to electrical energy, wind energy, light energy, sound energy, and mechanical energy. The first demonstrator achieves the conversion of chemical energy to electrical energy by leveraging endothermic/exothermic reactions and thermoelectric generators. Additionally, it combines a small fan, a light-emitting diode, and an electronic sound generator to enrich the forms of energy conversion. The conversions of chemical energy to wind energy, to light energy, and to sound energy are illustrated by connecting the thermoelectric generator’s output across a small fan, a light-emitting diode, and an electronic sound generator, respectively. The second demonstrator illustrates the conversion of electrical energy to chemical energy followed by the conversion of chemical energy to mechanical energy by powering a model car with self-fabricated hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells. item.title: ChatGPT as an Instructor’s Assistant for Generating Chemistry Images: A Study Using ChatGPT Images 2.0
item.description:
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

item.title: Gold-Catalyzed Oxidative Esterification: A Case Study to Challenge Students’ Fixed Thinking Pattern
item.description:
Abstract Esterification is a cornerstone reaction in chemistry and chemical engineering curricula, typically taught through the Fischer esterification pathway, i.e., the condensation of carboxylic acid with an alcohol to form an ester and water. Students are first exposed to this pathway in high school chemistry, and the concept is reinforced throughout their undergraduate studies, often leading them to develop a fixed thinking pattern that ester synthesis is assumed to proceed exclusively through this route. This work presents a case study designed to challenge this fixed thinking pattern using gold-catalyzed oxidative esterification. In this transformation, alcohols undergo oxidative coupling with O2 to form esters directly, without using carboxylic acid or its derivative as a starting material. For instance, benzyl alcohol self-couples to benzyl benzoate in water with O2 as the oxidant; when methanol is present, cross-coupling occurs to give methyl benzoate. The pedagogical design follows a cognitive conflict framework: students are first asked to identify ester synthesis methods, then are presented with the alternative pathway, and finally are guided to compare the two pathways. Implementation including an informal survey during a chemical engineering laboratory course (the ethyl acetate reactive distillation experiment) showed that students identified Fischer esterification as the default pathway. item.title: Beyond Point Allocation: Auditing Course-Objective Alignment and Item-Level Performance across a Two-Semester Organic Chemistry Sequence
item.description:
Abstract Course-assessment alignment is often judged from a blueprint that shows how many examination points are assigned to each course objective. Such a summary can be reassuring, yet it leaves unanswered what students are actually required to do. This study examined two consecutive final examinations in a 64 h undergraduate organic chemistry course for energy storage engineering majors at a Chinese university. The evidence base combined the official syllabus, examination blueprint, scoring guides, 119 scored subtasks, and regular final-examination records from 84 students in Semester 1 and 83 students in Semester 2. Scored subtasks were coded for course objective, revised-Bloom cognitive demand, organic chemistry task, intended difficulty, and contextual demand; student performance was analyzed at the 38 and 40 parent units for which scores were recorded. Point allocation closely matched the intended 40:60 distribution for Course Objectives 1 and 2 (44:56 and 38:62). In contrast, 99 of 100 points in Semester 1 and all 100 points in Semester 2 could be completed without using production, everyday-life, or engineering context. Item-level results further showed that observed difficulty did not increase monotonically across Bloom categories; several of the lowest score rates occurred on synthesis and selected multistep transformations. The findings show how a layered audit of alignment and student performance can reveal features that point allocation alone does not capture.

item.title: Analysis of Chemical Mixtures as a More Authentic Pedagogical Approach to Teaching 1H NMR Spectroscopy in Organic Chemistry Courses
item.description:
Abstract A pedagogical resource has been designed to situate the instruction of 1H NMR spectroscopy within a more authentic context through the interpretation of chemical mixtures. By shifting away from traditional “unknown structure elucidation” problems, this approach engages students with spectral data in a manner that more closely reflects genuine chemical practice. Mixture analysis is routinely employed by synthetic chemists to monitor reaction progress and evaluate product purity, thus this methodology provides realistic context for how spectroscopic evidence is used to inform decision-making in a research environment. This resource comprises a database of 1H NMR spectra of mixtures representing a broad range of organic transformations commonly taught in introductory organic courses including aldol condensation, alkene addition, electrophilic aromatic substitution, elimination, esterification, Grignard reactions, oxidation, reduction, reductive amination, and substitution. We illustrate how these materials can be scaffolded throughout the organic chemistry curriculum to align with students’ progressively developing competencies in mixture analysis and NMR interpretation. We also identify common difficulties encountered by students when interpreting chemical mixtures and present survey data indicating that students perceive mixture-based tasks as a more authentic application of spectroscopic data compared to conventional unknown structure elucidation exercises.

item.title: From Ancient Wisdom to Modern Practice: A High-School STEM Activity on Artemisinin Extraction with the Soxhlet Extractor
item.description:
Abstract STEM activities that integrate disciplinary knowledge with hands-on practice have gained increasing attention in science education. This study designed a high-school chemistry activity based on the Soxhlet extraction of crude artemisinin, comprising six sequential sessions that guided students through the crude extraction process. Students applied scientific principles by interpreting ancient chemical literature and understanding extraction and testing theories; mastered technological skills through hands-on operation of an extraction apparatus and chemical assays; developed mathematical competence via measuring reagents and calculating yield; and cultivated engineering thinking by designing experimental protocols and industrial production workflows. To evaluate the effectiveness of the activity, we administered a postactivity questionnaire and an achievement test. The results indicated that the activity effectively enhanced students’ conceptual understanding, practical skills, and learning interest, while also promoting interdisciplinary literacy.

item.title: From Carbon Dots to Food Freshness Indication: A Research-Inspired Undergraduate Laboratory Integrating Fluorescence Spectroscopy and Food Spoilage Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract Research-inspired laboratory experiences can help students connect molecular structure, spectroscopic behavior, and decisions made during real-sample analysis. In this 12 h upper-division experiment, fourth-year Pharmaceutical Engineering students used instructor-prepared nitrogen-doped carbon quantum dots (Clus-CQDs) as a pH-responsive fluorescent material for qualitative, storage-associated freshness indication in real food samples. Students recorded Fourier transform infrared and fluorescence spectra and interpreted instructor-provided transmission electron microscopy/high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy data. They then compared excitation- and solvent-dependent emission, related the pH-dependent fluorescence response to plausible protonation and deprotonation of surface groups, and examined responses to four representative spoilage-associated biogenic amines and to three protein-rich foods. The sequence from structural evidence to optical properties and then to application required students to distinguish a pH-dependent fluorescence response from analyte-specific recognition and to identify food-matrix and imaging factors that limit interpretation. The experiment was piloted with 18 students in three groups; paired pre- and postlab concept-question responses were retained for five students and are reported as descriptive evidence of student reasoning. item.title: Evaluating Generative AI in Chemistry Prelabs: Efficiency Gains without Measurable Learning Benefits
item.description:
Abstract The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has raised questions regarding their impact on students’ information literacy (IL) and cognitive processes. In this study, we investigated how generative AI influences undergraduate students’ performance and perceptions in an inorganic chemistry prelaboratory assignment consisting in gathering and elaborating information relevant to the experiments. Second-year chemistry students completed two prelab tasks: one with generative AI support and one without AI. Students reported that generative AI support significantly reduced time dedicated to prelab elaboration. They also perceived AI-assisted tasks as easier and faster, rated AI-generated information as less clear and precise than traditional sources, and frequently expressed concerns about its reliability. However, no statistically significant differences were observed in instructor-evaluated scores between AI-supported and non-AI prelabs. These results indicate that students predominantly valued AI for efficiency. Interpreted through a Cognitive Load Theory lens, the reduction in time and search effort is consistent with a possible decrease in task-related logistical demands.

item.title: Generative-AI-Assisted Development of Browser-Based Docking Notebooks: A ChatGPT “Vibe Coding” Methodology for Chemistry and Pharmacy Education
item.description:
Abstract Molecular docking is widely taught in medicinal chemistry and pharmacy programs, yet student participation is frequently limited by software installation barriers, platform incompatibilities, and uneven access to computational resources. This report describes a generative-AI-assisted (“vibe coding”) methodology in which ChatGPT is used to iteratively draft, refine, and debug Google Colab notebooks that deliver an install-free docking experience through a web browser. Because Colab executes Python in the browser and requires no local setup, the workflow can be run on laptops or mobile devices, supporting equitable access for students. Two notebooks are reported: (i) single-ligand docking to a single receptor with SMILES input, pH-aware structure preparation, autodetection of a docking box from a co-crystallized ligand when present, and student-editable sampling parameters (grid, exhaustiveness, poses, verbosity, seed) and (ii) a library-screening notebook that accepts a SMILES list, prepares ligands in parallel with pH control, executes batch docking, and exports ranked results for analysis. The central educational contribution is not only the notebook itself but a reproducible prompt → code → test loop that enables instructors to construct browser-deployable computational notebooks, which students with minimal coding experience can then run and modify at the parameter level while practicing verification, scientific reasoning, and responsible AI disclosure.
作者：Sayed Ahmed M. | DOI：10.1021/acs.jchemed.6c00083 | 类型：journal-article

item.title: Collaborative Interdisciplinary Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (ci-CURE) through Academic and Industry Partnerships
item.description:
Abstract The benefits of engaging undergraduates in research have been well documented. Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) offer a venue to extend the benefits of undergraduate research to a larger and more diverse group of students by making research accessible to all enrolled students and as such making scientific research more inclusive. Moreover, there is a growing recognition within the scientific community of the importance of equipping students with the ability to collaborate effectively in multidisciplinary teams to drive scientific advancement. Herein we report on the implementation of collaborative, interdisciplinary course-based undergraduate research experiences (ci-CURE) with academic and industry partners in an upper-division Measurement Techniques course sequence. Preliminary findings indicate that these collaborative projects were met with consistently positive collaborator feedback, fostered sustained partnerships, with many collaborators returning in subsequent semesters, and in several cases, generated publication-ready data for participating researchers, while also providing students with a positive and impactful learning experience. In addition, survey results revealed that repeated exposure to CUREs across courses supports cumulative gains in student competencies. This collaborative model of undergraduate research has the potential to be replicated and expanded within other chemistry departments seeking to help students see chemistry

item.title: Light-up Intracellular Mitochondrial G-Quadruplex Structures: Expanding the Understanding of Atypical Nucleic Acid Structures for Undergraduate Students
item.description:
Abstract In recent years, many atypical nucleic acid structures have been reported closely associated with the occurrence and development of various diseases. However, many undergraduate students remain largely unfamiliar with these structures. To broaden undergraduates’ understanding and reinforce their comprehension through hands-on practice, we have developed an undergraduate experiment using a fluorescent probe to visualize DNA G-quadruplexes (G4, an atypical nucleic acid structure). This probe features operational simplicity, strong stability, and intuitive visualization, which perfectly aligns with the technical criteria of ″low threshold, high safety, and strong feedback″ for undergraduate experimental teaching. First, using this probe, students can rapidly identify DNA sequences that form G4 structures through fluorescence spectroscopy. Subsequently, students can directly observe G4 structures in mitochondrial DNA (mtG4) of living cells via confocal microscopy, thereby transforming abstract theories of DNA structures into intuitive imaging results. item.title: Determining the Structure of the Oxalate Ion in Aqueous Solution: An Upper Division Laboratory Project Using IR Spectroscopy, Raman Spectroscopy, and DFT Calculations
item.description:
Abstract Although the planar D2h structure for the oxalate ion is found in solid metal oxalates with small cations, IR and Raman spectra of the oxalate ion in aqueous solutions and high-level theoretical calculations indicate the nonplanar D2d structure is more stable in systems with large cations or in these solutions. A laboratory exercise using attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, NMR, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to determine the structure of the oxalate ion in aqueous solutions has been developed and used three times in the physical chemistry laboratory at James Madison University (JMU). While the measured IR and Raman spectra are consistent with the D2d structure, DFT/B3LYP calculations using the integral equation formalism polarizable continuum model (IEFPCM) to model the intrinsic solvent interactions found a stable D2 structure that is only 300 J higher in energy than the D2d structure. In addition to showing that IR and Raman spectroscopies are complementary techniques for determining the structure of a molecule, this exercise shows that DFT calculations can provide additional information that is not easily determined using only experimental measurements. For example, students can explore the effect that solute–solvent interactions have on the structure of the ion in aqueous solution by adding explicit water molecules hydrogen bonded to the oxalate. item.title: The Use of Contact Angle in Conjunction with Dyne Tests: A Multimethod Surface Analysis Approach for Understanding Various Theoretical Concepts for an Upper-Division Undergraduate Course
item.description:
Abstract Concepts such as surface energy, contact angle, wettability, printability, critical surface tension of a material, etc. are pertinent across various fundamental scientific, engineering, technological, and industrial fields. Such concepts are widely researched, taught, and applied. However, these fundamental concepts at the undergraduate level are partly understood at best even in the well-rounded scientific disciplines. For students in cross-disciplinary domains with diverse and applied educational curricula these concepts can be perplexing. A sequential two-instrument methodology has been applied for hands-on learning of these concepts in an upper-division undergraduate instrumental analysis laboratory course in a polytechnic university, central coast California. Contact angle measurement along with dyne test were used to measure surface energy, contact angle, and wettability. This sequential two-stage material evaluation exercise introduces students to two different test methods utilized for qualitative and quantitative surface energy measurement of various polymers.

item.title: Using ChatGPT to Support Ninth-Grade Students’ Metaphor Construction in Chemistry and Sustainability
item.description:
Abstract This Activity describes a three-phase classroom protocol in which ninth-grade chemistry students construct metaphors for four sustainability concepts─green chemistry, ecological sustainability, ecological footprint, and carbon footprint─first independently and then with ChatGPT-4o support. Drawing on Conceptual Metaphor Theory and Structure Mapping Theory as design inspiration rather than as a hypothesis to be tested, the activity was built to give students two contrasting metaphor-construction experiences to compare and reflect on. It was implemented with 73 ninth-grade students across multiple class sections in a Turkish science high school chemistry course during a unit on sustainability. Students first generated metaphors independently, then used teacher-provided prompt templates to generate and select ChatGPT-supported metaphors, and finally completed a written reflection comparing both experiences. The metaphors and justifications students produced in each phase, together with their reflections, are presented as evidence of the kinds of thinking the activity elicits, along with practical guidance, materials, and adaptation notes for instructors.

item.title: Integrating Computational and Experimental Approaches: In Silico Design and In Vivo Validation of an Ergothioneine Biosynthetic Pathway in Escherichia coli
item.description:
Abstract This paper presents a modular, project-based learning (PBL) experiment designed for upper-division undergraduate laboratories in biochemistry, chemical biology, or synthetic biology. The project guides students through the complete cycle of metabolic engineering: from the computational design of a biosynthetic pathway to experimental implementation and analysis. Using production of the antioxidant ergothioneine in Escherichia coli as a case study, students engage in bioinformatics, molecular modeling, genetic engineering, microbial cultivation, and chemical analysis. The experiment emphasizes the connection between computational prediction and experimental validation, fostering critical thinking and interdisciplinary skills. Assessment data and student feedback indicate an enhanced understanding of the pathway design, enzyme function, and the iterative nature of scientific research.

item.title: From Consumers to Designers: Building Rule-Based Chatbots to Reinforce Chemistry Learning and Foster Critical AI Literacy
item.description:
Abstract This article describes an instructional approach that shifts secondary school participants from passive consumers of artificial intelligence to active designers by engaging them in building a closed-loop, rule-based chatbot. Implemented with 62 students (grades 8–12) in Georgia, the project required collaborative curation of chemistry content and programming of deterministic conversational logic. Unlike generative AI, this rule-based approach aligns with the rule-governed nature of core chemistry concepts such as stoichiometry and the mole concept. Pre- and post-test comparisons demonstrated substantial conceptual gains, particularly in abstract domains (+28% to +30%). Incorporating a social-contextual layer containing class-specific “insider knowledge”-triggered cognitive conflict that reduced uncritical trust in chatbot outputs from 70% to 15%. This approach offers secondary chemistry educators a practical strategy to simultaneously reinforce disciplinary understanding and foster critical digital literacy.
作者：Makaridze Maka | DOI：10.1021/acs.jchemed.6c01077 | 类型：journal-article

item.title: Adventures in Food Foams: An In-Class Activity Introducing Colloidal Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract We have developed an in-class activity for a nonmajor chemistry course with 19 students to introduce colloidal chemistry using food foams. By involving students in the preparation and tasting three foods and their ingredients, including Chantilly cream, Salzburger Nockerl, and French-style vanilla ice cream, participants experienced how the transformation of simple ingredients into food foams would greatly change the taste and texture of the resulting recipes. The amounts of air in the food foams were measured to help students understand the presence of air in each recipe preparation. We have found that students with food activity experience scored an average of 73.7% (N = 19) on the multiple-choice questions about colloidal chemistry on the final examination. Based on the in-class survey, the food activity was perceived as engaging. Further, half of the students who participated in the survey identified the effect of the transformation into food foams as the most valuable piece of knowledge from the food activity. item.title: Volumetric Titrations with (Non-)Visual Indicators: How Low-Cost Assistive Technology Can Make Existing Experiments More Accessible
item.description:
Abstract Quality education is one of the requirements for sustainable development, as identified by the United Nations. Achieving this goal requires educational practices that are accessible and understandable for all students, including those with disabilities. Traditional chemistry teaching experiments, such as volumetric titrations, often rely on visual indicators to demonstrate chemical changes in solution and are often used to teach chemical equilibria. However, different students may perceive color changes differently, affecting their learning experience. To address this challenge, this paper presents a framework for creating alternative representations of solution color change in real time during volumetric titration experiments, relying on low-cost and easy-to-fabricate assistive technologies. Our proposed framework allows for the real-time translation of solution color changes to other sensory stimuli, like sound, and can be used to support accessible education in accordance with the principles of the universal design for learning. We take this approach to neutralization and redox volumetric titrations, making these practices, which rely on visual indicators of the equivalence point, more accessible in educational chemistry laboratories.

item.title: Opening the Potentiostat “Black Box”: A Low-Cost and Highly Integrated Instrumentation Demonstration for Undergraduates
item.description:
Abstract Potentiostats are central to electrochemical measurements, yet their operating principles are rarely taught in undergraduate chemistry education. Consequently, students often treat the instrument as a “black box” that converts input parameters into electrochemical curves without understanding the underlying hardware logic and feedback principles. Herein, we report a visually intuitive and accessible instructional demonstration that opens this black box by combining low-cost potentiostat assembly with cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements using screen-printed electrodes (SPEs). This activity provides a complete learning workflow encompassing two- and three-electrode systems, operational-amplifier feedback circuits, electronic-component assembly, graphical software operation, instrument verification, and CV measurements. A Lego-like modular kit further allows each student group to independently build a functional potentiostat. The use of highly integrated, inexpensive SPEs in place of conventional electrochemical cells and individual electrodes further simplifies the experimental setup and reduces material costs. Evaluated through activity completion and postdemonstration exercises, this demonstration integrates electrochemistry, instrumentation, electronic circuit, and data analysis into one interdisciplinary activity, at a cost low enough for wide classroom adoption.

item.title: Development, Implementation and Iterative Refinement of a Three-Dimensional Assessment Framework for a Research-Integrated Chemistry Laboratory Course
item.description:
Abstract Assessment of research-integrated chemistry laboratory courses requires approaches that capture both team outcomes and individual contributions. This study reports the development, implementation and iterative refinement of a three-dimensional assessment framework integrating teacher assessment, group peer assessment, and individual contribution ratios. A preliminary version was piloted in a surfactant chemistry elective course, and the refined framework was implemented across three cohorts (2021 to 2023, N = 73) in a research-integrated experiment involving the synthesis of sodium dodecyl sulfate and the determination of its critical micelle concentration. Grade records and questionnaire responses were analyzed. Teacher and group peer assessments were strongly correlated, although peer scores were systematically higher than teacher scores in the two earlier cohorts. Course grades were higher in later cohorts; however, because cohort membership is confounded with changes in implementation, this pattern is reported descriptively and not interpreted as evidence of improved performance. Students reported highly positive perceptions of innovativeness, helpfulness, and fairness, together with high self-ratings of ability development. These perception measures are exploratory single-item indicators and exhibit ceiling effects, so they reflect student experiences rather than verified gains in ability. item.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence into a Context-Based Electrochemistry Laboratory: Supporting Student Reasoning in Corrosion Kinetics
item.description:
Abstract Tafel polarization analysis can be used to teach corrosion kinetics in upper-division physical chemistry and materials science laboratories, but implementing it through fixed procedures and automated fitting may limit students’ engagement with the underlying electrochemical principles. This work describes a context-based electrochemistry laboratory that integrates a large language model (LLM) as an analytical scaffold rather than a source of ready-made answers. The experiment was implemented with 60 third-year (fifth-semester) undergraduates in engineering-related majors. Students worked in groups of three, with each student attending one laboratory session consisting of three 45-min class periods. Within a materials-selection scenario for marine bridge components, students compared Q235 plain carbon steel and Q235NH weathering steel in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. Throughout the “AI + Lab Session,” DeepSeek was used to generate candidate SOPs, propose troubleshooting hypotheses, and clarify spreadsheet-based Tafel analysis, while students evaluated AI-generated operating parameters, performed Tafel polarization measurements, used AI-supported reasoning to troubleshoot instrumental problems, manually analyzed raw polarization data in spreadsheet software, and connected corrosion kinetics with a 30-year life-cycle cost analysis. item.title: Industry-Driven Dual Mentorship for Progressive Competency Development in the Principles of Chemical Engineering Course
item.description:
Abstract Principles of Chemical Engineering, as a core professional course in chemical engineering education, faces several challenges, including insufficient student motivation for deep learning, limited capability for engineering application, and inadequate awareness of engineering ethics. Guided by the OBE (Outcome-Based Education) concept, a university–enterprise dual-mentor team systematically integrated the ARCS (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, Satisfaction) motivation model, the CDIO (Conceive, Design, Implement, Operate) engineering education framework, and constructivist learning theory to implement comprehensive teaching reforms. These reforms involved reorganizing course content around chemical production processes, developing diverse teaching resources, establishing a three-stage teaching model, implementing a progressive and immersive engineering ethics education pathway, and constructing a multidimensional evaluation mechanism. Based on these initiatives, a new teaching paradigm characterized by “Industry-Driven Dual Mentorship for Progressive Competency Development” was established. The observed reform outcomes were associated with improvements in students’ learning motivation, engineering application capability, and engineering ethics awareness, indicating a potentially transferable approach for cultivating professionals in green chemical engineering.

item.title: Simulation-Based Approaches in Chemical Engineering Experiments
item.description:
Abstract The virtual experimental simulation approach provides an effective means to educate high-level chemical engineering students with analytical and design capabilities. The proposed study analyzes the challenges in Experiments of Chemical Engineering Principles and existing simulation experiment software in most of the Chinese universities. In response, a reform plan was proposed that embraces a student-centered educational philosophy while emphasizing the guiding role of instructors. Based on this reform plan, a virtual simulation system was developed to enable the students to engage in autonomous, in-depth, inquiry-based experiments. The system offers efficient grade management tools for teachers and supports multiplatform operations to meet the modern educational demands. The system has been piloted and promoted across various universities in China with feedback from both instructors and students. Results demonstrate that virtual simulation software effectively supports the development of Experiments in Chemical Engineering Principles to train chemical engineering professionals.
